analysis.one_liner: Adds transparency rules and cost-first procedures that slow down and weaken federal rulemaking.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 236-179 on a near party-line vote, but the Senate never brought it to the floor, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill packages four regulatory changes together. It requires agencies to publish online, every month, the rules they plan to propose or finalize, with cost estimates, and it blocks any rule from taking effect until that information has been posted for at least six months. It rewrites the Administrative Procedure Act so agencies must generally adopt the cheapest rule that meets their statutory goals, hold formal hearings with cross-examination before rules costing $1 billion or more, and makes it easier for companies to challenge rules in court. It also expands analyses of how rules affect small businesses and requires agencies to publish proposed court settlements about regulations 60 days before filing them.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies regulated by federal agencies gain the most: rules would take effect later, agencies would be steered toward the cheapest option, formal hearings and broader court review would give industry more openings to challenge or block rules, and proposed settlements with agencies would become public and contestable before they are finalized.

how_it_helps.text: Each agency must submit a monthly report on every rule it expects to propose or finalize in the coming year, including cost estimates and job effects, and the OMB regulatory office must post this information online within 30 days.

No rule can take effect until the required information has been posted online for at least six months, with exceptions for emergencies, criminal law enforcement, national security, and trade agreement rules.
Agencies must adopt the least costly rule that meets their statutory objectives, and may choose a costlier one only if the extra benefits justify the extra cost.

Before adopting any rule costing $1 billion or more a year, agencies must hold a formal hearing with cross-examination of the evidence, and advance notice at least 90 days before proposing major rules.
Courts may no longer defer to an agency's interpretation, cost-benefit analysis, or guidance if the agency did not follow the bill's procedures, making rules easier to overturn in litigation.

Agencies must publish proposed consent decrees and settlements 60 days before filing them with a court and allow public comment, addressing the practice of advocates suing an agency and settling on terms behind closed doors.

analysis.who_pays: Workers, consumers, and communities who rely on federal protections. Rules on workplace safety, air and water, consumer finance, and food would face at least a six-month delay before taking effect, and the cheapest-rule mandate and expanded litigation openings would make it harder to issue and keep strong protections.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers and consumers relying on federal protections

drawbacks.text: The six-month posting delay applies to every rule, so even routine protections would be held back unless an emergency exception applies, delaying relief for people waiting on finalized rules.
Requiring agencies to adopt the least costly rule that meets statutory objectives pushes decisions toward the minimum protection the law allows, and cost estimates are often contested.

Formal hearings with cross-examination and broader judicial review would make rulemaking slower and more litigation-heavy, which its critics said would paralyze agencies and benefit parties able to afford extended legal fights.

Supporters' strongest point in return: the transparency provisions have genuine public value, since today much of what agencies plan and how they estimate costs is scattered, and publishing it monthly could let the public and affected workers see rules coming earlier.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency pieces are a real, if modest, public good. But the bill's core — the cheapest-rule mandate, formal hearings, six-month delay, and limits on judicial deference — is designed around reducing the cost and power of federal regulation for regulated companies, and the burden falls on people who depend on those rules. A cleaner transparency-only bill would have delivered the upside without slowing protections across the board.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House on a near party-line vote in February 2014, went to the Senate's Homeland Security committee, and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Oversight and Government Reform Committee reported the bill on a 19-15 vote in February 2014, and the Judiciary Committee was discharged so it could move.

The House debated it under a rule covering one hour per bill and rejected a Democratic motion to recommit the bill with instructions to exempt rules that save tax dollars, help small businesses and veterans, prevent discrimination, or protect consumers, by a vote of 187-229.
Final passage in the House was 236-179, with 226 of 231 Republicans voting yes and only 10 of 199 Democrats doing so.
The Senate received the bill on March 4, 2014, read it twice, and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, where it stayed.
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, with no Senate vote ever taken.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a Senate vote, existing rulemaking procedures continued unchanged, and rules on workplace safety, consumer finance, and the environment kept taking effect without the six-month delay or the cheapest-rule mandate. Ordinary people who depend on those protections were better off; regulated companies lost the slower, more challengeable rulemaking system the bill would have given them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People relying on federal safety rules

industries.industry: Regulated industries (manufacturers, energy, finance, and other rule targets)
industries.note: The bill would give regulated companies a six-month delay before any rule takes effect, steer agencies toward the cheapest rule, require formal hearings before billion-dollar rules, and widen the grounds for suing to overturn rules. Those gains come directly at the cost of slower, weaker protections for workers, consumers, and the environment.

The Regulatory Flexibility title requires agencies to analyze cumulative and indirect impacts on small businesses, consult the SBA's advocacy office before major proposals, and consider alternatives that ease burdens on small entities. Many small firms, however, are also protected by the same rules this process would delay.

The Sunshine title requires proposed consent decrees and settlements to be published and commented on 60 days before filing, and lets agencies more easily modify old decrees. That makes it harder for these groups to win negotiated deadlines compelling agencies to issue rules on schedule.
